Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

mirtverse 0.3.0

  • The paper describing mirtverse is out as a preprint on PsyArXiv (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/j9ya7_v1). It is cited in the README, in citation("mirtverse") and in CITATION.cff.

  • Turkish materials: A Turkish introduction page (articles/tr, linked as “Türkçe” in the navbar and from the README) and a Turkish version of the two-page cheat sheet (cheatsheet/mirtverse-cheatsheet-tr.pdf). The cheat sheet source is data-raw/cheatsheet/cheatsheet-tr.html, and data-raw/cheatsheet/build.js now renders both languages.

  • New article and printable poster, “Which IRT model?”: A one-page flowchart from what one item score looks like (0/1, ordered categories, unordered options or ideal-point items) to a model and its itemtype, with structure questions (dimensions, testlets, groups, item features, response times, latent classes), fit checks and a QR code back to the article. The poster source is in data-raw/which-model/.

  • The mirtverse agent: A plugin for Claude Code that lets Claude analyze test data with mirtverse on the user’s computer. Install it in Claude Code with /plugin marketplace add okanbulut/mirtverse and /plugin install mirtverse@mirtverse. It brings five skills (analyze-test, check-dif, review-items, write-report, setup), an irt-analyst subagent, and a new MCP server, mv_agent_server(), whose tools fit and compare models, check items, test DIF, score people, draw plots that Claude can see, interpret the results, write the HTML report, run other R code, and save every step as one reproducible R script. Models are kept between sessions. New mv_agent_init() sets up a folder without the plugin (a CLAUDE.md with the agent’s instructions and a .mcp.json), and mv_mcp_config() has a new mode = "analysis" for Claude Desktop, Codex and other MCP clients. A new article, “The mirtverse agent for Claude”, explains it.

  • Three narrated video demos (about 90 seconds each, with captions): The workbench tour, the AI Hub and the thesis kit. They are on the home page, on a new “Video demos” page (Start here menu) and in the AI Hub, thesis kit and “New to R” articles.

  • New cite_methods() drafts the Methods paragraph of an IRT analysis in APA style: Software versions, the model and estimation method, the model comparison from select_model(), overall and item fit, reliability and removed items, with an alphabetical reference list. It prints, returns text, or writes Markdown or a Word file. A new “Thesis kit” article walks from item responses to that paragraph.

  • Workbench: The “Test summary” table on the Explore tab no longer errors with current mirt, which renamed the total-score columns of itemstats().

  • New article “Adopt mirtverse for your course” with a sample 12-week syllabus to edit (Word and PDF), a setup checklist and a GitHub form for instructors to tell us about their course. New article “Case study: A certification exam, from field test to pass/fail” follows a fictional board through eight recorded decisions and links a downloadable technical report (PDF and HTML). The home page now highlights the AI in measurement hub with an animated graphic.

  • The website has a new front door. The home page opens with a one-line summary, a four-step workflow diagram, a grid of real outputs (dashboard, item health card, Wright map, DIF plot) and a “Find your way in” table, and a new “Start here” menu has a short path for students, instructors, testing programs, researchers and people new to R. A new Gallery article shows every figure and output with its code. Links to the site now show a share image on LinkedIn, Bluesky and X, and the README has a “How to cite” box near the top.

  • New, experimental simulate_llm_respondents() asks a language model to answer multiple-choice items as described respondents (“personas”) would, and new compare_synthetic() checks the answers against real data: Difficulty, its order across items, the variety of response patterns and item-total correlations. The example recordings for mv_llm_replay() include a run on itemtext that shows the usual problems (items too easy, alike personas answering alike, stereotyped groups), and chapter 17 of the book has a box on it.

  • New copy_workshop() copies a kit for a one-day workshop on AI in measurement: Slides, a facilitator’s guide and a README, built around Labs 7 to 10. A new article, “AI in measurement: A one-day workshop”, describes it.

  • The instructor toolkit can teach AI in measurement on an instructor’s own data. new_lab() and swap_lab_data() take item_info (one row per item, with its text or its item family) and scores (machine and human scores of written answers), and lab_section_types() has three new sections: "item-features" (item_features() and predict_difficulty()), "aig" (calibrate_families()) and "ai-scoring" (agreement_report() and ai_audit()). As in the other sections, every answer is computed from the data. lab_data() returns the new tables.

  • The instructor MCP server has a new guide, guide("ai-content"), on teaching AI in measurement, a new prompt, “Teach AI in measurement”, and the new item_info and scores arguments in its new_lab and swap_lab_data tools.

  • The course map has an optional four-week module on AI in measurement (weeks 13 to 16, Labs 7 to 10 and book chapters 13 to 18) and a one-day workshop schedule.

  • New ai_audit() audits an AI component in one call and returns flags in the pipeline’s block / review / info style: Human and machine agreement, overall bias, agreement within groups, differential scoring (machine minus human at the same human score, against a reference group, beyond sampling error), drift across administrations or engine versions, DIF on the test as scored (on AI-scored items for review, on others for information), and results of predict_difficulty() (leakage), calibrate_families() (isomorphism) and agreement_report(). It has print(), tidy() and autoplot() methods.

  • New validity_argument() drafts a Kane-style validity argument from an audit: Claims, AI-specific threats, evidence and a status for the scoring, generalization, extrapolation and decision inferences, with what is still owed. format() gives HTML or Markdown, and mv_report() takes it directly as an extra section.

  • New Lab 10, run_lab("ai-audit"): Students audit an engine-scored science test over two years (the new aiscored and aiscored_cr data) before its scores are released. The book has a new chapter, “Validity, fairness and governance of AI” (ai-validity in book_chapters()).

  • New item_model() writes an item model for automatic item generation: A stem, key and distractors as templates with R expressions in braces, the values of each variable and constraints. Printing it shows how many combinations meet the constraints and how many give four different options. New generate_isomorphs() fills one or more models, leaves out (or flags) combinations with identical options, and returns the items with the values they came from. New calibrate_families() summarizes the calibrated difficulties of each family: Mean, within-family SD corrected for estimation error, a 95% interval for a new isomorph, the field-test size the family mean can replace, and whether the family is isomorphic.

  • New Lab 9, run_lab("aig"): Students fix an item model, calibrate a field test of 60 generated items (the new aigfield and aigfield_items data), find a family split by regrouping and two items with identical options, and test family means on held-out items. The book has a new chapter, “Generating items” (aig in book_chapters()), with one-step family calibration in mirt (mixedmirt()) and eirm.

  • New item_features() describes items by features of their text: Length, sentences and readability of the stem, its numbers, decimals and negations, the length of the options, whether the key is the longest option, how far numeric distractors are from the key, and each item’s most similar other item, to find near-duplicates. Everything runs in base

  • New predict_difficulty() predicts item difficulty from features with an LLTM (two-step explanatory IRT), a lasso and a random forest, all in base R, and compares them by cross-validation, with random folds or whole groups (such as item families) held out. It flags features that look leaked from the field test, shows the estimation error in b as a floor, and has tidy(), autoplot() and predict() methods.

  • New Lab 8, run_lab("item-text"): Students predict the difficulty of the 192 itemtext items from their text, find miskeyed items and near-duplicates, catch a leaky feature, hold out whole item models, and decide what predictions can replace. The book has a new chapter, “What item text tells us” (item-text in book_chapters()), with the one-step LLTM in mirt.

  • New train_scorer() trains an automated scoring engine on human-scored text: A ridge regression on words and two-word phrases, in base R, with the penalty chosen by cross-validation. It runs offline, predict() scores new answers, tidy() shows the word weights, and it plugs into score_open(). New agreement_report() compares machine and human scores overall, by group and by item: Exact and adjacent agreement, QWK, SMD, correlation and PRMSE, with a verdict against mv_rules() and an autoplot() method.

  • New Lab 7, run_lab("auto-scoring"): Students train an engine on essays, judge it on new students, find why it underscores English language learners, and decide how much of the scoring it should do. The book has a new chapter, “Automated scoring” (auto-scoring in book_chapters()).

  • essays is harder to score by machine, as real answers are: Language learners misspell more content words and drop articles, some answers state an idea the wrong way round with the right words, and raters are a little less consistent (human-human QWK about 0.8). The example recordings were rebuilt to match.

  • The online book has a new part, AI in measurement, with two chapters: “Machine learning through an IRT lens” (prediction versus measurement, the 2PL as a logistic regression on a latent predictor, overfitting and cross-validation) and “Large language models as a colleague” (what is sent to a model, checking generated items, reproducibility with recorded responses). Both build offline with mv_llm_replay(). book_chapters() lists them as ml-lens and llms, and the AI Hub menu links to them.

  • New mv_llm_replay() answers every language model request (mv_ask(), generate_items(), verify_items(), score_open(), review_packet(ai_screen = TRUE)) from a file of recorded responses, so lessons and examples run with no API key or internet connection and give the same result every time. mv_llm_record() records a live session for later replay and mv_llm_recordings() lists what a file covers. The package ships example recordings for the calls in system.file("replay", "examples.R", package = "mirtverse"); their responses were written by hand and include deliberate mistakes for the checks to catch.

  • Two new teaching datasets for the AI Hub. itemtext has the text and 2PL field-test statistics of 192 simulated numeracy items from 12 item families, for predicting difficulty from item text and calibrating item families. essays has 1,600 short science explanations by 400 students, scored 0 to 4 by raters, for automated scoring. Both have planted problems that lab_truth("itemtext") and lab_truth("essays") reveal.

  • New AI Hub for psychometricians who want to learn how artificial intelligence fits into measurement, with its own menu in the site navbar. It has a landing page with a learning path and examples of the AI features already in mirtverse (“AI Hub: Artificial intelligence for psychometricians”), a table that translates more than 40 machine learning terms into their closest psychometric ideas (“Machine learning for psychometricians: A translation table”), and an annotated reading list. The glossary has a new “AI in measurement” section with 13 terms.

  • New online book, Item Response Theory with mirt and mirtverse, at https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/book/. Twelve chapters follow the weeks of the course map, from classical item analysis to cut scores and reporting. Each has learning goals, glossary links, two worked examples on different data, exercises with solutions and a pointer to the matching lab. The bookdown source is in book/, every example loads its data in one labelled chunk so instructors can swap in their own, and the pkgdown workflow builds the book into the site. The site navbar links to it.

  • New instructor toolkit for teaching with your own data, with a guide on the website (“The instructor toolkit”). new_course() sets up a course folder and course_materials() lists what is in it. new_lab() builds an interactive learnr lab on any response dataset (a data frame or a CSV, Excel, SPSS, Stata or SAS file), with sections from lab_section_types() whose text, answer checks and quiz answers are computed from the data, so swap_lab_data() can replace the data later. add_lab_section(), add_lab_exercise(), add_lab_question(), remove_lab_section() and lab_outline() edit a lab; copy_lab() makes an editable copy of a built-in lab; copy_chapter(), new_chapter() and swap_chapter_data() do the same for chapters of the mirtverse book. check_material() runs every exercise’s solution through its check (and can render the lab) before students see it, and preview_lab() opens it.

  • New MCP server for instructors: mv_mcp_server() connects an AI assistant (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, the OpenAI Agents SDK or ChatGPT) to a course folder, so instructors can revise labs, chapters and notes, build labs on their own data, and adapt existing materials (including ltm, eRm, TAM and irtQ code) to mirtverse by describing what they want. The assistant reads and edits files only inside the course folder, every change is backed up and can be undone, it looks up real mirtverse functions instead of guessing, and it runs check_material after each change. Lab and chapter tools wrap the instructor toolkit. mv_mcp_config() prints the settings to paste into each client. See the new article “An AI assistant for your course materials”.

  • New teaching lab, “Scoring open-ended responses”: run_lab("open-ended"). Six science tasks were scored 0-4 by two human raters each and by an automated scoring engine. Students check rater agreement (exact, adjacent, quadratic weighted kappa), find a severe and an inconsistent rater, resolve final scores with third reads, compare the PCM, GPCM and GRM, collapse rubric categories with disordered steps, and decide whether the engine can replace a human reader, including a subgroup fairness check. The new openended data come with lab_truth("openended").

  • New teaching lab, “Designing an adaptive test”: run_lab("cat-design"). A college wants to replace its 40-item placement test with a CAT. Students look at where the item bank is informative, run one CAT by hand, simulate 500 students, and weigh test length and precision against item exposure (randomesque selection), content balancing and the stopping rule. The new catbank data (a 180-item calibrated bank) come with lab_truth("catbank").

  • New teaching lab, “Linking two forms”: run_lab("linking"). A licensure exam’s pass rate jumps on a new form, and students find out why: They calibrate both forms, link them through common items with the mean-sigma method, catch an anchor item that drifted, compare separate and concurrent calibration, and carry the pass mark over to the new form with IRT true-score equating. The new linking data (two forms in a common-item nonequivalent groups design) come with lab_truth("linking").

mirtverse 0.2.0

Assessment pipeline

  • New assessment pipeline (first phase). mv_pipeline() starts a pipeline that takes a test from response data to a technical report in stages, with a gate of checks after each stage: add_responses() scores and screens the data (miskeyed items, missing data, straight-lining, rapid guessing, sparse categories), calibrate() fits the model and checks convergence, model fit, local dependence, item fit, parameter ranges, DIF (Mantel-Haenszel and standardized mean difference with the ETS A/B/C rules) and reliability, and pipeline_report() writes the HTML report with a section listing every flag and decision. Flags are info, review or block; they warn by default, and with strict = TRUE open review and block flags stop the next stage until a decision is recorded with acknowledge() or override(), or the item is removed with drop_items(). flags() lists them, and mv_rules() holds every threshold, which users can change by name. mv_report() gains an extra argument for additional sections.

  • Blueprint and item generation for the assessment pipeline (stages 0 and 1). set_blueprint() records the construct, content cells with target counts, item types, score use and target reliability, and flags empty cells and a missing score use. generate_items() writes multiple-choice items (with keys and option rationales) and open-ended items (with rubrics and anchor responses) for each cell through ellmer, using the provider set up with mv_ask_setup(), and verify_items() has an independent model call answer each item without the key. add_items() adds items written by people. The checks flag invalid or disputed keys, weak distractors, incomplete rubrics, near-duplicates, thin blueprint coverage and hard reading levels, and the pipeline report gains blueprint and item development sections. mv_rules() gains duplicate_sim and coverage_ratio.

  • Item review and field-test design for the assessment pipeline (stages 2 and 3). review_packet() writes a review form with one row per item and reviewer (optionally after an AI bias and accessibility screen), and read_reviews() reads the decisions back, sets each item’s status by majority and flags items with too few reviewers, alignment disagreements, sensitivity concerns, revision requests, low reviewer agreement (Fleiss’ kappa) and missing provenance. design_field_test() spreads the approved items over forms with anchor items, and flags small samples per item, too few anchors, cells without an anchor and poor simulated parameter recovery. mv_rules() gains min_reviewers, review_kappa, n_rasch, n_2pl, n_3pl and recovery_rmse.

  • Item banks and linking for the assessment pipeline (stage 6). mv_bank() starts an item bank from a calibrated model or pipeline, link_to_bank() puts a new calibration on the bank’s scale through anchor items (Stocking-Lord, Haebara, mean-sigma, mean-mean or fixed-anchor calibration) and flags drifting anchors, too few anchors and unusual linking constants, and bank_items() adds the new items to the bank. The pipeline report gains a linking section, and mv_rules() gains min_anchors, min_anchor_share, anchor_displacement, link_slope_min and link_slope_max.

  • Test forms for the assessment pipeline (stage 7). assemble_forms() builds one or more fixed forms by automated test assembly (eatATA), with a content blueprint, enemy items and parallel forms; simulate_cat() simulates a computerized adaptive test with mirtCAT; and assemble_mst() assembles a two-stage multistage test and simulates its routing. The checks flag unbuildable forms, blueprint and enemy violations, non-parallel forms, imprecise forms or CATs, over-exposed and unused items, shallow banks and misrouting. The pipeline report gains a forms section, and mv_rules() gains parallel_tol, cat_sem, cat_bias, max_exposure, unused_share, bank_depth, mst_routing and min_group_n. eatATA and mirtCAT are suggested packages.

  • Cut scores for the assessment pipeline (stage 8). set_cuts() records cut scores on the ability or summed-score scale (or from a standard-setting panel’s ratings) and estimates classification accuracy and consistency, overall and by cut, with kappa and false positive and negative rates: By Lee’s (2010) method for summed-score cuts and Rudner’s (2001) method for ability cuts, for the calibrated test or a fixed form. It flags low accuracy or consistency, imprecise cuts and panel disagreement, and the pipeline report gains a cut score section. item_map() gives the ordered item booklet for Bookmark standard setting. mv_rules() gains cut_accuracy, cut_consistency, cut_sem and panel_sd.

  • Scoring for the assessment pipeline (stage 9). score_open() scores open-ended responses against their rubrics with a language model through ellmer, or with any trained model that has a predict() method, and checks the machine scores against human scores (Williamson, Xi and Breyer, 2012): Too few double-scored responses, low human-human or machine-human quadratic weighted kappa, shifted score distributions and subgroup differences. Short, off-topic and low-confidence responses are routed to human scoring, and the final scores can join the response data for a mixed-format calibration. score_persons() estimates abilities and flags low reliability and extreme scores. mv_rules() gains n_validation, qwk_min, qwk_drop, score_smd, subgroup_smd, min_confidence, min_words and max_se.

  • Test security for the assessment pipeline (stage 10). check_security() looks for item preknowledge (a likelihood ratio test of leaked against secure items), item leakage across administration windows (proportion correct up, response times down), parameter drift from the bank, answer copying (identical incorrect answers against their expected number), aberrant response times (lognormal residuals), sites with too many flagged test takers and unusual score gains. Respondent-level evidence stays in p$security$persons; flags and the report give counts only. mv_rules() gains preknowledge_alpha, leak_p, leak_rt, drift_a, drift_b, copy_alpha, rt_resid, rt_share, site_alpha and gain_sem.

  • Bank monitoring for the assessment pipeline (stage 12). monitor_bank() records each administration in the item bank (item exposure and marginal reliability by window) and checks the bank over time: Items over-exposed in consecutive windows, content cells with too few active items, reliability falling from its first value, and items unused for a year. retire_items() retires bank items or sends them back to review. mv_rules() gains exposure_windows, cell_depth, reliability_drop and unused_days.

  • The workbench gains a Pipeline tab: Run the data through the assessment pipeline’s intake and calibration gates (or load a saved pipeline), follow the stage tracker, record decisions on flags, drop items and recalibrate, and download the pipeline and its report. The SAT12 example in the workbench now loads correctly.

  • New article, “An assessment pipeline from blueprint to bank monitoring”, takes the certexam data through every stage of the pipeline.

Coming from other IRT packages

  • New mirtify() translates code written for ltm, eRm, TAM and irtQ into mirt code, with a note on every difference between the packages (for example CML versus MML in eRm, the scaling constant D in irtQ, and the number of quadrature points). It covers the model functions and their follow-ups: Person scores, item and person fit, information, plots and Andersen’s likelihood-ratio test. run = TRUE also runs the translated code. mirtify_crosswalk() lists every supported function, and the new article “Moving from ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ to mirt” walks through examples and shows how closely the translated models match the originals.

  • The homepage has a mirtify() section with a short example.

Teaching and learning

  • New interactive teaching labs for measurement courses, built with learnr. run_lab("model-choice") opens Lab 1, “Choosing a model the board can defend”: Students score a certification exam, find a miskeyed item, check dimensionality, compare the Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models, check item fit and local dependence, and justify a model, with feedback on every decision and a summary of their choices at the end. run_lab("decisions") opens Lab 2, “From parameters to decisions”: Reading item parameters, precision at the pass mark, choosing a scoring method, classification accuracy, DIF between English and French candidates, a memo to the board, and a reveal of the truth behind the data. list_labs() lists the labs. The new certexam data (with certexam_key) are simulated with known problems planted for the labs; lab_truth() reveals them for instructors. The article “Teaching labs for measurement courses” introduces the labs for students, followed by an instructor guide and an answer key.

  • New article, “A course map for instructors”: A suggested 12-week IRT syllabus that links each week to articles, labs, functions and datasets.

  • New teaching lab, “Is the test fair? Detecting DIF”: run_lab("fairness"). Students investigate a complaint that a provincial numeracy test is biased against English language learners: They separate impact from DIF, run Mantel-Haenszel and IRT likelihood-ratio DIF tests, purify the anchor, judge how much the DIF matters for students’ scores with differential test functioning, and plan a content review. The new numeracy data (with numeracy_items) have DIF planted on purpose, and lab_truth("numeracy") reveals it. The “Teaching labs” article covers the new lab, with its answers in the answer key at the end.

  • New article, “Glossary of IRT terms”: 87 terms in plain language, grouped from the basic ideas to test design, each with the mirtverse or mirt function that computes it and a figure where one helps. Every term has a stable anchor (for example glossary.html#discrimination) for linking from course materials.

  • A printable two-page cheat sheet (PDF), linked from the navbar and the README: Page 1 covers analysis and sharing by task, page 2 the assessment pipeline stages, gates and flags.

Sharing results

  • New mv_dashboard() builds a read-only ‘shiny’ dashboard of your results for people who do not use R. Choose the panels (summary, items with health cards, item curves with an ability slider, information, Wright map, score distribution and conversion table, and optionally person scores, DIF and response times), add a title and logo, and run it. export_dashboard() saves it as an app.R folder ready for shinyapps.io or Posit Connect. The saved dashboard holds summaries only, never the item responses, and holds individual scores only when you add the "persons" panel.

  • export_dashboard(format = "html") saves the dashboard as one self-contained HTML file that needs no server, no R and no internet connection. The item table, item curves with the ability slider, item information and person lookup stay interactive.

  • The article “Sharing results with a dashboard” is now a full guide: When to use a dashboard rather than the workbench or the report, every panel, sharing as one HTML file or as a Shiny app, privacy, and a live example dashboard to open.

Scripts from plain language

  • New mv_ask() writes a complete, commented analysis script from a plain-language request such as “fit a 2PL, check DIF by gender and make a report”. Requests are understood by Claude, OpenAI GPT or a local Ollama model (set up once with mv_ask_setup()), or offline by a built-in keyword parser that asks follow-up questions. Only a column summary is ever sent; anonymize = TRUE hides column names and dry_run = TRUE shows exactly what would be sent. Scripts can be refined (mv_ask(scr, "use a 3PL instead")) and are built from an analysis plan (mv_plan()): Data preparation, model fitting or selection, fit checks, DIF, scores, graphics, item cards, reports and response times. run_script() runs it, optionally after a dry run on simulated data with the same structure, and save_script() writes it to a file. profile_data() shows the column summary that is the only information shared with an AI model. The workbench now writes its code with the same templates.

  • mv_ask() reads plans from local models that write text before the JSON (such as Qwen on Ollama), and accepts a plan with no extra steps (for example DIF requested without a grouping variable), instead of falling back to the keyword parser.

  • The internal request benchmark (mirtverse:::ask_benchmark()) no longer stops when a provider cannot be reached; those requests are scored as wrong and the reason is printed.

  • New article, “mv_ask(): From a sentence to a tested R script”, shows the workflow and benchmarks Claude, GPT and local Qwen models against the keyword parser.

Differential item functioning

  • New dif() tests every item for differential item functioning between groups in one call, with likelihood-ratio tests, adjusted p-values and expected-score effect sizes. gg_dif() plots the effects or the item curves by group, interpret() describes the results, and mv_report(dif = ) adds a DIF section to the report.

  • dif() keeps the order of a factor’s levels, so the first level is the reference group (earlier development versions sorted the groups alphabetically).

Response times

  • fit_rt() gains the normative threshold rules flag_method = "nt15" and "nt20" for rapid guessing (15% and 20% of each item’s mean response time), next to "nt10", and the workbench offers all three. Following Wise and Ma (2012), the item thresholds of all three rules are now capped at 10 seconds; change the cap with the new nt_max argument (nt_max = Inf removes it). The thresholds used are returned in $thresholds.

  • fit_rt() no longer fails when some persons have no item responses. mirt drops those rows from the fitted data; fit_rt() now keeps them, and their response times still inform speed.

Other changes

  • The package website moved to https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/.

  • mirtverse can be cited through its Zenodo DOI; see citation("mirtverse") or CITATION.cff.

  • “Get started” gains sections on dashboards, mv_ask() and the teaching labs, and the workbench article covers the NT10, NT15 and NT20 rules.

mirtverse 0.1.0

First release.

  • launch_workbench(): A seven-step Shiny app that writes reproducible R code.
  • select_model(): Compares candidate IRT models and explains the recommendation.
  • interpret() and interpret_prompt(): Plain-language summaries of mirt results.
  • tidy(), glance(), augment() and item_table() for mirt models.
  • ggplot2 graphics: gg_trace(), gg_info(), gg_wright(), gg_itemfit(), gg_q3(), gg_scores(), gg_empirical() and autoplot().
  • item_card() and item_cards(): Item health cards with a traffic-light status.
  • mv_report(): A self-contained HTML report.
  • fit_rt() and sim_rt(): Joint modelling of responses and response times with rapid-guessing flags, response time effort and l_t person fit.
